desc: In June and July 2023 the Galileo Project conducted a fully funded expedition, budgeted at approximately $1.6 million, to the Pacific Ocean site of CNEOS 2014-01-08 - a 0.45-metre bolide that entered the atmosphere near the northeast coast of Papua New Guinea on 8 January 2014 and which Amir Siraj and Avi Loeb had argued, in The Astrophysical Journal in November 2022, had an apparently interstellar velocity. The team dragged a magnetic sled across the seabed at a location determined from seismometer data and recovered several hundred sub-millimetre spherules, which Loeb's group classified in Research Notes of the AAS (31 January 2024) and Chemical Geology (December 2024) as including a distinct composition they labelled 'BeLaU' - enriched in beryllium, lanthanum and uranium - which they argued was inconsistent with solar-system materials. The counter-argument arrived quickly and in the ordinary way. Patricio Gallardo argued in Research Notes of the AAS in October 2023 that anthropogenic coal ash could contaminate a micro-meteoritic underwater search. Steve Desch posted critiques in November 2023 and March 2024. Fernando et al. published in Geophysical Journal International in March 2024 showing that the seismic signal used to localise the search was more consistent with truck traffic than with an ocean impact - meaning the sled may have been dragged in the wrong place entirely. Rudraswami, Singh and Pandey published a re-evaluation of the spherules' proposed origin in Chemical Geology in March 2025. This expedition matters to the board as the control case: it is what a genuine, funded, public physical-recovery attempt looks like, including its failure modes, and every part of the argument - claim, rebuttal, re-analysis - happened in the peer-reviewed literature within eighteen months. That is the standard against which seventy years of unpublished government custody should be measured.
